title: “The boss took the chilies not me”, Homebirth in undocumented Myanmar migrant women: A mixed methods study of Strengthening Migrant Access to Reproductive Healthcare in Thailand (SMARH-T) initiative
content:
by Mary Ellen Gilder, Jasper Ko Ko Aung, May Myo Thwin, Prapatsorn Misa, May Mon Mon Theint, Nan San Wai, Pitak Sila, Htet Htet Win, Naw Hser Eh Moo, Taco Jan Prins, Nay Win Tun, Aung Myat Min, Ahmar Hashmi, François Nosten, Daniel M. Parker, Rose McGready

Homebirth for undocumented migrants can be dangerous and results in statelessness for the child. This study identified factors associated with homebirth along the Thailand–Myanmar border and explored women’s perceptions of homebirth. We conducted a sequential explanatory mixed methods study within free antenatal care (ANC) clinics for migrant workers in Thailand. ANC records and birth outcomes were collected for women registered at outreach clinics (March-2021 to February-2024). Women who gave birth at home (October-2023 to September-2024) completed a semi-structured survey on reasons, consequences, and preferences. Interviews with women, village health workers, and staff were conducted in June to July 2025. Among 1,593 women, 183 (11.5%) delivered at home. In adjusted analyses, each additional ANC visit was associated with a 34% reduction in the odds of homebirth (AOR 0.66 per visit, 95% CI 0.60–0.72). Primiparous women had lower odds of homebirth than multiparous women (AOR 0.46, 95% CI 0.27–0.79), and among multiparous women, prior caesarean delivery reduced homebirth (AOR 0.21, 95% CI 0.06–0.72). Although most (70%) women who birthed at home expressed a preference for facility birth, rapid labor onset, transportation difficulties, and fear of police checkpoints were the main reasons for delivering at home. Not receiving a birth certificate was the greatest perceived consequence of homebirth, though obstetric complications were also mentioned. Better preparation to reach facilities was the main recommendation to prevent homebirth. Most undocumented migrant women in this setting prefer facility delivery. Insufficient ANC, the strongest predictor for homebirth, is likely to both influence place of delivery and be a proxy for women’s trust and ability to overcome barriers to access the healthcare system. Providing support to all women around birth planning and extra support to women with fewer ANC visits may increase facility births.
